stem: A breastfeeding client is returning to work and wants to maintain milk production while separated from the infant. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Express milk about as often as the infant normally drinks breast milk while they are apart.
options.B: Stop breastfeeding after returning to work because pumping cannot support milk production.
options.C: Expect milk production to fall sharply whenever daytime separation begins, regardless of milk removal.
options.D: Avoid discussing workplace pumping because federal protections never apply to nursing employees.

rationale: CDC guidance updated in 2026 advises people who are away from their baby to pump about as often as the baby normally drinks breast milk; regular milk removal helps the body continue making the amount of milk the baby needs. Most covered U.S. employees also have federal rights to reasonable pump breaks and a private non-bathroom space for up to one year after birth, subject to statutory coverage and exemptions. A is correct.
educational_objective: Teach milk-expression frequency that supports continued lactation during separation and accurately describe current U.S. workplace pumping protections.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); U.S. Department of Labor (DOL)
source_document_title: Breastfeeding and Returning to Your Workplace; Pumping Breast Milk; FLSA Protections to Pump at Work
source_version_date: CDC March 13, 2026 and February 24, 2026; DOL revised January 2026
source_locator: CDC — How often to pump/return-to-work considerations; DOL — What You Should Know
source_claim_supported: When separated from the infant, pump about as often as the baby normally drinks breast milk to help maintain supply; most covered employees have reasonable-break and private-space protections for pumping at work.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — breastfeeding and return to work

source_original.stem: A nurse is counseling a breastfeeding client who is returning to work about maintaining milk supply. The nurse should advise the client that:

options.A: Express milk regularly at intervals similar to usual feeds to help maintain supply while apart
options.B: Stop breastfeeding after returning to work because pumping rarely maintains milk production
options.C: Expect milk supply to decline sharply whenever daytime separation from the infant begins
options.D: Assume workplace protections do not apply and that scheduled milk-expression breaks are unavailable

source_original.rationale: Regular milk expression (pumping) at intervals similar to the infant's typical feeding schedule can help maintain milk supply while a breastfeeding mother is separated from her infant during work hours. Additionally, U.S. federal law (under the Fair Labor Standards Act, as amended) provides certain workplace protections and accommodations for breastfeeding employees to express milk.
source_original.source_detail: U.S. DOL nursing-mother break-time protections plus regular milk expression to maintain supply; reviewed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Updated to CDC 2026 lactation guidance and DOL 2026 workplace-protection language, avoided claiming universal legal coverage, and made the keyed action the exact CDC milk-removal recommendation.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Milk-expression frequency and legal protections are directly supported; legal wording is qualified for coverage/exemptions.

distractor_audit.D: False absolute; most covered employees have protections.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A uniquely answers the milk-supply teaching question.
audit_findings.blueprint: Breastfeeding education fits Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked both CDC 2026 pages and DOL revised 2026 page; A remains unique.
